tagline: Nine beach communities, a reef light and an artist’s winter home
intro: Broward County’s A1A Scenic Highway follows the Intracoastal Waterway through nine beach communities on Florida’s southeast coast. The Florida Scenic Highways program designated the 32-mile corridor on July 20, 2009; its description brings together beach scenery, historic sites, parks and piers. Native dune plants and sea turtle nests are among the sights along its beaches.

The A1A name grew out of a numbering problem. Florida designated the route State Road 1 in 1945, reflecting its position as the easternmost major north–south road in the new grid. Confusion with parallel U.S. Highway 1 led the State Road Board to order a change in November 1946. A1A kept the number 1 in its place in that grid.

Traveling south from Deerfield Beach, the corridor reaches Hillsboro Beach’s lighthouse, then Pompano Beach and the underwater archaeological preserve at Lauderdale-by-the-Sea. Bonnet House anchors the historic sites in Fort Lauderdale. The corridor also includes the 17th Street Causeway, part of U.S. 1 and Dania Beach Boulevard. At Dania Beach, A1A joins U.S. 1 for 3.4 miles and passes the Fort Lauderdale–Hollywood airport. The southward journey continues through Hollywood toward the Miami-Dade county line.

moments.title: Hillsboro Inlet Light
moments.text: An iron skeleton tower marks the northern limit of the Florida Reef at Hillsboro Inlet. Requests for a lighthouse began in 1884 and met 17 rejections before Congress authorized construction in 1901. The tower was first lit on March 8, 1907. Its black upper section and white lower section were chosen for daytime visibility: white against trees, black against the sky. A failed rotating mechanism shut down the big light in 1992; a local campaign persuaded the Coast Guard to restore it rather than remove the original lens. The large light was relit in January 1999.
moments.notice: The tower’s iron framework encloses a central stair column.

moments.title: SS Copenhagen
moments.text: Copenhagen’s voyage from Philadelphia to Havana ended on a reef south of Hillsboro Inlet in May 1900. The cargo steamer carried almost 5,000 tons of coal. When she struck Pompano Dropoff, reversing the engine failed to free her. Two days later a salvage vessel began unloading coal, with local people helping transfer the cargo; the ship stayed on the reef. The wreck became a Florida Underwater Archaeological Preserve in June 1994. A plaque at its southern end records that designation, beneath the water off Lauderdale-by-the-Sea. The steamer had been built in England in 1898.

moments.title: Bonnet House
moments.text: An artist’s studio was the first building completed at Bonnet House. Hugh Taylor Birch gave the property to his daughter Helen and her husband, artist Frederic Clay Bartlett, in 1919. Bartlett, a self-taught architect, designed the main house as his interpretation of Caribbean plantation architecture and used it as a winter home. His later wife, Evelyn, deeded the property to the Florida Trust for Historic Preservation in 1983. The buildings share the estate with dunes, mangrove wetlands, a freshwater slough and maritime forest. In the drawing room, the mahogany ceiling came from a large log washed ashore in a storm.
